_**Just Men!**_ is an American game show that aired on NBC Daytime from January 3 to April 1, 1983. The show starred Betty White, who won an Emmy award for her work on the show, with Steve Day announcing. It pitted two female contestants who were asked to predict answers to a series of yes/no questions posed previously to a panel of seven male celebrities.
The show was created and produced by Rick Rosner, who was producing _CHiPs_ at the time for NBC, and was a joint production of Rosner Television, Century Towers Productions, and Orion Television. This was one of two collaborations among the three entities. Rosner was later responsible for reviving another NBC game show, _Hollywood Squares_, which he co-produced with Century Towers with Orion distributing.
The general format of the game, in which the contestant determines whether a celebrity answers "yes" or "no" to a question, is similar to Heatter-Quigley's _The Celebrity Game_, which aired on CBS from 1964 to 1965.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Men!#cite_note-1)
This was also the first game show in history to have two female contestants playing prior to another short-lived, male-oriented game show _Mind of a Man_ hosted by comedian DeRay Davis that also featured two female contestants playing that aired on Game Show Network (GSN) in 2014.

Two female contestants, one usually a returning champion, competed for a chance to win a car displayed on the stage. At the beginning of each episode, the host used the car's actual ignition key to start it, then dropped that key and six others into a clear plastic box fitted with internal chutes to mix them. One key was given to each panelist; throughout the main game, a panelist stopped taking any active role once a contestant had claimed his key. The champion played first in every round.
The contestants were presented with a question to which at least two panelists had answered "yes." Each contestant questioned the panel for one minute, using a provided list of topic-related questions, then attempted to select one panelist she believed had said "yes." A correct guess awarded that panelist's key. If both contestants guessed correctly, the round ended at that point. Otherwise, they took turns asking one question at a time to any one panelist of their choice and predicting who said "yes"; the round ended once a total of two keys had been claimed.
The contestants were presented with a question to which at least two of the remaining five panelists had answered "no." They questioned the panel as in Round 1 and attempted to guess who had answered "no." As in Round 1, a correct guess awarded the panelist's key; however, a miss gave the key to the opponent. Each contestant had one turn.

### Round 3 (Catch-Up Round)
[edit]
A third question was presented, with no announcement as to how many of the remaining three panelists had answered either way. The contestants took turns questioning one panelist at a time and predicting his response. A correct guess awarded that panelist's key and allowed the contestant to steal one key from her opponent, while a miss gave the key and the steal to the opponent.
This round ended after all seven keys had been claimed, at which point the contestant holding more keys won the game. The loser received one consolation prize for each key she held, but was guaranteed a minimum of one prize.
The champion selected one of the keys she held for every main-game victory to that point, and could select one more key if she had claimed all seven. She sat in the driver's seat of the car, with the panelist(s) originally associated with the chosen key(s) gathered around or sitting in it, and tried one at a time in the ignition. If the car started, she won it and retired undefeated; if not, the host identified the correct key and opened the trunk with it, revealing a prize the champion received.
Any champion who won seven consecutive games automatically won the car and retired undefeated.
_Just Men!_ premiered on NBC January 3, 1983, along with two other game shows: _Hit Man_ and a revival of _Sale of the Century_. The program aired at 12:00 noon Eastern/11:00 a.m. Central, though some stations such as WRC-TV in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") aired the program on next-day tape delay.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Men!#cite_note-Shales1983-2) Like many game shows in this time slot,_[citation needed_]_Just Men!_ suffered from low affiliate clearances, as many larger markets aired newscasts at noon by 1983. The show lasted just thirteen weeks, ending its run on April 1, 1983. It was replaced in its time slot by _The New Battlestars_, which also ended after thirteen weeks.

### Round 3 (Catch-Up Round)
_Just Men!_ aired opposite _Family Feud_ on ABC nationwide, and _The Young and the Restless_ on CBS outside the Eastern Time Zone.[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Men!#cite_note-3)
Despite the show's short run, Betty White made television history. She became the second woman to be nominated for the Daytime Emmy Award for Outstanding Game Show Host by herself (Susan Stafford was nominated in 1978) and the first to win the award in 1983, when she was voted ahead of Dick Clark and Richard Dawson. White was nominated for a second straight year in 1984, but finished behind Bob Barker and Dawson.
Tom Shales of _The Washington Post_ called the show "the litmus test for people who think the TV show that can make them physically ill hasn't been invented."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Men!#cite_note-Shales1983-2) He criticized the nature of questions asked during the show and wrote, "White, a talented light comedian, is terribly demeaned by this role, which has her hobbling about from man to man as they utter answers or remarks that are supposedly uproarious."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Men!#cite_note-Shales1983-2)
1.   ↑CBS had allocated the 12:00 Noon time slot to local programming in Eastern Time. In some Eastern markets, such as New York City, _Just Men!_ aired opposite _Tattletales_, which aired at 12:00 Noon instead of 4 p.m. ET._[citation needed_]

1.   ↑_The Encyclopedia of TV Game Show_, by David Schwartz, Steve Ryan and Fred Wostbrock (Checkmark Books, 1999, pp.37-38)

Just Men!
Network: NBC
Broadcast History: NBC daytime January 3rd to April 1st, 1983
Host: Betty White
Announcer: Steve Day  
Just Men! was a very highly unusual short-lived game show, where two contestants were women while the celebrity guests were seven men, hence the name of the show, Just Men!
Despite a short-lived run, Betty White won a Daytime Emmy for her work on the show as she was the first female to ever win a Daytime Emmy for Outstanding Game Show Host.
Both this show and Hit Man (with guest panelist Peter Tomarken as host) have premiered on the same day on January 3rd, 1983 and ended the same day on April 1, 1983.

_**Just Men!**_ is an American game show that aired on NBC Daytime from January 3 to April 1, 1983. The show starred Betty White, who won an Emmy award for her work on the show, with Steve Day announcing. It pitted two female contestants who were asked to predict answers to a series of yes/no questions posed previously to a panel of seven male celebrities.
The show was created and produced by Rick Rosner, who was producing _CHiPs_ at the time for NBC, and was a joint production of Rosner Television, Century Towers Productions, and Orion Television. This was one of two collaborations among the three entities. Rosner was later responsible for reviving another NBC game show, _Hollywood Squares_, which he co-produced with Century Towers with Orion distributing.
The general format of the game, in which the contestant determines whether a celebrity answers "yes" or "no" to a question, is similar to Heatter-Quigley's _The Celebrity Game_, which aired on CBS from 1964 to 1965.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Men!#cite_note-1)
This was also the first game show in history to have two female contestants playing prior to another short-lived, male-oriented game show _Mind of a Man_ hosted by comedian DeRay Davis that also featured two female contestants playing that aired on Game Show Network (GSN) in 2014.
texts.1:
Two female contestants, one usually a returning champion, competed for a chance to win a car displayed on the stage. At the beginning of each episode, the host used the car's actual ignition key to start it, then dropped that key and six others into a clear plastic box fitted with internal chutes to mix them. One key was given to each panelist; throughout the main game, a panelist stopped taking any active role once a contestant had claimed his key. The champion played first in every round.
The contestants were presented with a question to which at least two panelists had answered "yes." Each contestant questioned the panel for one minute, using a provided list of topic-related questions, then attempted to select one panelist she believed had said "yes." A correct guess awarded that panelist's key. If both contestants guessed correctly, the round ended at that point. Otherwise, they took turns asking one question at a time to any one panelist of their choice and predicting who said "yes"; the round ended once a total of two keys had been claimed.
The contestants were presented with a question to which at least two of the remaining five panelists had answered "no." They questioned the panel as in Round 1 and attempted to guess who had answered "no." As in Round 1, a correct guess awarded the panelist's key; however, a miss gave the key to the opponent. Each contestant had one turn.
texts.2:
### Round 3 (Catch-Up Round)
[edit]
A third question was presented, with no announcement as to how many of the remaining three panelists had answered either way. The contestants took turns questioning one panelist at a time and predicting his response. A correct guess awarded that panelist's key and allowed the contestant to steal one key from her opponent, while a miss gave the key and the steal to the opponent.
This round ended after all seven keys had been claimed, at which point the contestant holding more keys won the game. The loser received one consolation prize for each key she held, but was guaranteed a minimum of one prize.
The champion selected one of the keys she held for every main-game victory to that point, and could select one more key if she had claimed all seven. She sat in the driver's seat of the car, with the panelist(s) originally associated with the chosen key(s) gathered around or sitting in it, and tried one at a time in the ignition. If the car started, she won it and retired undefeated; if not, the host identified the correct key and opened the trunk with it, revealing a prize the champion received.
Any champion who won seven consecutive games automatically won the car and retired undefeated.
_Just Men!_ premiered on NBC January 3, 1983, along with two other game shows: _Hit Man_ and a revival of _Sale of the Century_. The program aired at 12:00 noon Eastern/11:00 a.m. Central, though some stations such as WRC-TV in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") aired the program on next-day tape delay.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Men!#cite_note-Shales1983-2) Like many game shows in this time slot,_[citation needed_]_Just Men!_ suffered from low affiliate clearances, as many larger markets aired newscasts at noon by 1983. The show lasted just thirteen weeks, ending its run on April 1, 1983. It was replaced in its time slot by _The New Battlestars_, which also ended after thirteen weeks.

### Round 3 (Catch-Up Round)
_Just Men!_ aired opposite _Family Feud_ on ABC nationwide, and _The Young and the Restless_ on CBS outside the Eastern Time Zone.[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Men!#cite_note-3)
Despite the show's short run, Betty White made television history. She became the second woman to be nominated for the Daytime Emmy Award for Outstanding Game Show Host by herself (Susan Stafford was nominated in 1978) and the first to win the award in 1983, when she was voted ahead of Dick Clark and Richard Dawson. White was nominated for a second straight year in 1984, but finished behind Bob Barker and Dawson.
Tom Shales of _The Washington Post_ called the show "the litmus test for people who think the TV show that can make them physically ill hasn't been invented."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Men!#cite_note-Shales1983-2) He criticized the nature of questions asked during the show and wrote, "White, a talented light comedian, is terribly demeaned by this role, which has her hobbling about from man to man as they utter answers or remarks that are supposedly uproarious."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Men!#cite_note-Shales1983-2)

_**Just Men!**_ is an American game show that aired on NBC Daytime from January 3 to April 1, 1983. The show starred Betty White, who won an Emmy award for her work on the show, with Steve Day announcing. It pitted two female contestants who were asked to predict answers to a series of yes/no questions posed previously to a panel of seven male celebrities.
The show was created and produced by Rick Rosner, who was producing _CHiPs_ at the time for NBC, and was a joint production of Rosner Television, Century Towers Productions, and Orion Television. This was one of two collaborations among the three entities. Rosner was later responsible for reviving another NBC game show, _Hollywood Squares_, which he co-produced with Century Towers with Orion distributing.
The general format of the game, in which the contestant determines whether a celebrity answers "yes" or "no" to a question, is similar to Heatter-Quigley's _The Celebrity Game_, which aired on CBS from 1964 to 1965.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Men!#cite_note-1)
This was also the first game show in history to have two female contestants playing prior to another short-lived, male-oriented game show _Mind of a Man_ hosted by comedian DeRay Davis that also featured two female contestants playing that aired on Game Show Network (GSN) in 2014.

Two female contestants, one usually a returning champion, competed for a chance to win a car displayed on the stage. At the beginning of each episode, the host used the car's actual ignition key to start it, then dropped that key and six others into a clear plastic box fitted with internal chutes to mix them. One key was given to each panelist; throughout the main game, a panelist stopped taking any active role once a contestant had claimed his key. The champion played first in every round.
The contestants were presented with a question to which at least two panelists had answered "yes." Each contestant questioned the panel for one minute, using a provided list of topic-related questions, then attempted to select one panelist she believed had said "yes." A correct guess awarded that panelist's key. If both contestants guessed correctly, the round ended at that point. Otherwise, they took turns asking one question at a time to any one panelist of their choice and predicting who said "yes"; the round ended once a total of two keys had been claimed.
The contestants were presented with a question to which at least two of the remaining five panelists had answered "no." They questioned the panel as in Round 1 and attempted to guess who had answered "no." As in Round 1, a correct guess awarded the panelist's key; however, a miss gave the key to the opponent. Each contestant had one turn.

### Round 3 (Catch-Up Round)
[edit]
A third question was presented, with no announcement as to how many of the remaining three panelists had answered either way. The contestants took turns questioning one panelist at a time and predicting his response. A correct guess awarded that panelist's key and allowed the contestant to steal one key from her opponent, while a miss gave the key and the steal to the opponent.
This round ended after all seven keys had been claimed, at which point the contestant holding more keys won the game. The loser received one consolation prize for each key she held, but was guaranteed a minimum of one prize.
The champion selected one of the keys she held for every main-game victory to that point, and could select one more key if she had claimed all seven. She sat in the driver's seat of the car, with the panelist(s) originally associated with the chosen key(s) gathered around or sitting in it, and tried one at a time in the ignition. If the car started, she won it and retired undefeated; if not, the host identified the correct key and opened the trunk with it, revealing a prize the champion received.
Any champion who won seven consecutive games automatically won the car and retired undefeated.
_Just Men!_ premiered on NBC January 3, 1983, along with two other game shows: _Hit Man_ and a revival of _Sale of the Century_. The program aired at 12:00 noon Eastern/11:00 a.m. Central, though some stations such as WRC-TV in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") aired the program on next-day tape delay.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Men!#cite_note-Shales1983-2) Like many game shows in this time slot,_[citation needed_]_Just Men!_ suffered from low affiliate clearances, as many larger markets aired newscasts at noon by 1983. The show lasted just thirteen weeks, ending its run on April 1, 1983. It was replaced in its time slot by _The New Battlestars_, which also ended after thirteen weeks.

### Round 3 (Catch-Up Round)
_Just Men!_ aired opposite _Family Feud_ on ABC nationwide, and _The Young and the Restless_ on CBS outside the Eastern Time Zone.[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Men!#cite_note-3)
Despite the show's short run, Betty White made television history. She became the second woman to be nominated for the Daytime Emmy Award for Outstanding Game Show Host by herself (Susan Stafford was nominated in 1978) and the first to win the award in 1983, when she was voted ahead of Dick Clark and Richard Dawson. White was nominated for a second straight year in 1984, but finished behind Bob Barker and Dawson.
Tom Shales of _The Washington Post_ called the show "the litmus test for people who think the TV show that can make them physically ill hasn't been invented."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Men!#cite_note-Shales1983-2) He criticized the nature of questions asked during the show and wrote, "White, a talented light comedian, is terribly demeaned by this role, which has her hobbling about from man to man as they utter answers or remarks that are supposedly uproarious."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Men!#cite_note-Shales1983-2)

_**Celebrity Big Brother**_, also known as _**Big Brother: Celebrity Edition**_,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-1) is a spin-off series of the American version of the Dutch reality television franchise _Big Brother_. This season aired during the winter of the 2017–18 network television season on CBS and was the second American _Big Brother_ season to air outside the usual summer television season, the first being _Big Brother 9_ in 2008. Julie Chen returned as host, with Allison Grodner and Rich Meehan returning as executive producers. The series is produced by Fly on the Wall Entertainment in association with Endemol Shine North America. The first season premiered on February 7, 2018.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-tvline-2)

The promotional logo was released on December 20, 2017. The logo is similar to that used for _Big Brother 19_, with the word "celebrity" added.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-3) The first teaser was also released the same day.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-4) In January 2018 official photos of the house and backyard were released through a press release and an Instagram livestream with Julie Chen.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-6) On January 28, 2018, the official cast was announced during the 60th Annual Grammy Awards.
The first season officially concluded on February 25, 2018, when Marissa Jaret Winokur beat Ross Mathews by a final jury vote of 6 to 3. Ross was also later named _America's Favorite HouseGuest_.
On May 12, 2018, CBS renewed the spin-off for a second season.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-7)

After the first season of the British version of _Big Brother_ proved to be a success in the ratings for Channel 4, the network collaborated with the BBC for the first British season of _Celebrity Big Brother_ in aid of Comic Relief. The season ran for a condensed run of eight days and featured six British celebrities moving into the house used for the first British season.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-42) Due to the success of the first celebrity edition, a second season was ordered and shown exclusively on Channel 4 in November 2002. The celebrity version took a two-year break before returning for its third season in 2005, and became a regular staple alongside the regular British version. Starting with the third season, the show began to feature celebrities outside the United Kingdom alongside well known British celebrities. Many notable American celebrities have since taken part in the British version of _Celebrity Big Brother_.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-GlobalTV-43)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-AmericansInUKCBB-2-44) American actor Gary Busey took part in the fourteenth season in the summer of 2014 and became the first American celebrity to win _Celebrity Big Brother_ in the United Kingdom._[citation needed_]

An American version of _Celebrity Big Brother_ has been speculated since 2002, along with a celebrity version of _Survivor._[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-CBB-2002-1-45) In an interview, Julie Chen and CBS CEO Leslie Moonves revealed talks of a celebrity edition of _Big Brother_ as far back as _Big Brother 2._[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-InterviewTHR-46) It was rumored that CBS was looking to air a celebrity edition in the fall after _Big Brother 3_ with radio personality Howard Stern speculated as a possible houseguest.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-CBB-2002-2-47) Chen revealed that Paris Hilton had agreed to do it and Roseanne Barr initially agreed to take part, but then backed out.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-InterviewTHR-46) Barr would later take part in another celebrity spin-off of _Big Brother_ called _Big Brother: Celebrity Hijack_ in the United Kingdom in 2008, where she watched over a group of non-celebrity housemates for a day, set tasks and talked to them in the Diary Room.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Roseanne-BBCH-48)

Julie Chen announced on September 7, 2017, during a live double eviction episode of _Big Brother 19_ that _Celebrity Big Brother_ would air sometime during the winter, before the twentieth season of _Big Brother_ in the summer of 2018. CBS later confirmed via a press release that Julie Chen would return to host the new season, and Allison Grodner and Rich Meehan will be executive producers. The season will be produced by Fly on the Wall Entertainment in association with Endemol Shine North America.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Press1-49)
On September 13, 2017, it was revealed by Chen that her husband, CBS chief executive Leslie Moonves, forced her to take a pay cut for the celebrity edition to happen. Moonves stated, "You shouldn't be expected to be paid as if it's a full series. It's a condensed version."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-tvguide-50)
The format of the show remained similar to the American version of _Big Brother_. Competitions for Head of Household and Power of Veto had been confirmed to returned for this edition along with live evictions.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-tvline-2) On December 1, 2017, CBS revealed that the series would premiere on February 7, 2018, and wrap on February 25, 2018.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-51)

_Celebrity Big Brother_ was a condensed version of the game and would not last as long as a regular season of _Big Brother_, with episodes only shown over two weeks instead of three months.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-tvguide-50)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-52) Unlike the parent series Jury members were not sequestered separately and were allowed to return to the outside world as well as watch the show.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-53)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-54) Beginning with an incident that led to a lawsuit in _Big Brother 2_ when HouseGuest Justin Sebik got drunk and threatened fellow HouseGuest Krista Stegall by holding a knife to her throat, there has been an alcohol restriction in the house.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-55)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-56) The alcohol restriction was lifted for the Celebrity HouseGuests.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-57)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-58) The space in the backyard was reduced to allow production to constantly perform construction for competitions but still allow 24/7 access for the HouseGuests.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-59) For the celebrity version of America's Favorite HouseGuest,

the term Favorite Celebrity HouseGuest was also being used interchangeably.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-60)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-61) For the first time since the beginning of the American series, five players were featured in the season's finale night versus the usual three.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-62)

The main television coverage of _Celebrity Big Brother_ was screened on CBS during the winter of the 2017–18 network television season. CBS decided to schedule the spin-off during the February 2018 sweeps period to counterprogramNBC's coverage of the 2018 Winter Olympics.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Press1-49) Episodes aired on Sundays, Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays with two special episodes on Thursday, February 8 and Saturday, February 24. Most episodes aired for one hour and aired from 8:00–9:00 p.m. EST; the Friday episodes and the season finale, however, ran for two hours each (from 8:00–10:00 p.m. EST).[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Air_dates-63) The live Internet feeds returned for the American version of _Celebrity Big Brother_ as part of CBS All Access.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Press1-49)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-InterviewTHR-46) Alongside the weekly shows on CBS, the companion series _Big Brother: After Dark_ returned on Pop under the title _Celebrity Big Brother: After Dark_. The show provided live coverage nightly from inside the House.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Press1-49)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-64)

#### International broadcasts
[edit]
Promotional logo created for use in Australia that resembles the logo of Australian adaptation of _Big Brother_ from 2012 to 2014.
Global announced on December 20, 2017, that the broadcaster had acquired the rights to air _Celebrity Big Brother_ in Canada.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Broadcast-GlobalCAN-65) Global has broadcast the American version of _Big Brother_ since its launch in 2000.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-BBCPR-66)Nine Network confirmed they would air the season in Australia under the name _Celebrity Big Brother U.S._.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Australia-1-67) Nine created a special logo for the show resembling the eye logo of the ninth through eleventh seasons of Australian adaptation that previously aired on the network.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-68) Episodes were "fast-tracked" and available on their streaming service 9Now shortly after their American airing with televised broadcast on 9Go! starting February 11, 2018.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Australia-1-67) Due to low ratings episodes were moved from the 9:30pm timeslot to 11:30pm effective February 14, 2018.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-69)

_**Celebrity Big Brother**_, also known as _**Big Brother: Celebrity Edition**_,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-1) is a spin-off series of the American version of the Dutch reality television franchise _Big Brother_. This season aired during the winter of the 2017–18 network television season on CBS and was the second American _Big Brother_ season to air outside the usual summer television season, the first being _Big Brother 9_ in 2008. Julie Chen returned as host, with Allison Grodner and Rich Meehan returning as executive producers. The series is produced by Fly on the Wall Entertainment in association with Endemol Shine North America. The first season premiered on February 7, 2018.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-tvline-2)

The first season officially concluded on February 25, 2018, when Marissa Jaret Winokur beat Ross Mathews by a final jury vote of 6 to 3. Ross was also later named _America's Favorite HouseGuest_.
On May 12, 2018, CBS renewed the spin-off for a second season.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-7)

texts.8: After the first season of the British version of _Big Brother_ proved to be a success in the ratings for Channel 4, the network collaborated with the BBC for the first British season of _Celebrity Big Brother_ in aid of Comic Relief. The season ran for a condensed run of eight days and featured six British celebrities moving into the house used for the first British season.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-42) Due to the success of the first celebrity edition, a second season was ordered and shown exclusively on Channel 4 in November 2002. The celebrity version took a two-year break before returning for its third season in 2005, and became a regular staple alongside the regular British version. Starting with the third season, the show began to feature celebrities outside the United Kingdom alongside well known British celebrities. Many notable American celebrities have since taken part in the British version of _Celebrity Big Brother_.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-GlobalTV-43)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-AmericansInUKCBB-2-44) American actor Gary Busey took part in the fourteenth season in the summer of 2014 and became the first American celebrity to win _Celebrity Big Brother_ in the United Kingdom._[citation needed_]
texts.9: An American version of _Celebrity Big Brother_ has been speculated since 2002, along with a celebrity version of _Survivor._[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-CBB-2002-1-45) In an interview, Julie Chen and CBS CEO Leslie Moonves revealed talks of a celebrity edition of _Big Brother_ as far back as _Big Brother 2._[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-InterviewTHR-46) It was rumored that CBS was looking to air a celebrity edition in the fall after _Big Brother 3_ with radio personality Howard Stern speculated as a possible houseguest.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-CBB-2002-2-47) Chen revealed that Paris Hilton had agreed to do it and Roseanne Barr initially agreed to take part, but then backed out.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-InterviewTHR-46) Barr would later take part in another celebrity spin-off of _Big Brother_ called _Big Brother: Celebrity Hijack_ in the United Kingdom in 2008, where she watched over a group of non-celebrity housemates for a day, set tasks and talked to them in the Diary Room.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Roseanne-BBCH-48)
texts.10:
Julie Chen announced on September 7, 2017, during a live double eviction episode of _Big Brother 19_ that _Celebrity Big Brother_ would air sometime during the winter, before the twentieth season of _Big Brother_ in the summer of 2018. CBS later confirmed via a press release that Julie Chen would return to host the new season, and Allison Grodner and Rich Meehan will be executive producers. The season will be produced by Fly on the Wall Entertainment in association with Endemol Shine North America.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Press1-49)
On September 13, 2017, it was revealed by Chen that her husband, CBS chief executive Leslie Moonves, forced her to take a pay cut for the celebrity edition to happen. Moonves stated, "You shouldn't be expected to be paid as if it's a full series. It's a condensed version."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-tvguide-50)
The format of the show remained similar to the American version of _Big Brother_. Competitions for Head of Household and Power of Veto had been confirmed to returned for this edition along with live evictions.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-tvline-2) On December 1, 2017, CBS revealed that the series would premiere on February 7, 2018, and wrap on February 25, 2018.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-51)
texts.11: _Celebrity Big Brother_ was a condensed version of the game and would not last as long as a regular season of _Big Brother_, with episodes only shown over two weeks instead of three months.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-tvguide-50)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-52) Unlike the parent series Jury members were not sequestered separately and were allowed to return to the outside world as well as watch the show.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-53)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-54) Beginning with an incident that led to a lawsuit in _Big Brother 2_ when HouseGuest Justin Sebik got drunk and threatened fellow HouseGuest Krista Stegall by holding a knife to her throat, there has been an alcohol restriction in the house.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-55)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-56) The alcohol restriction was lifted for the Celebrity HouseGuests.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-57)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-58) The space in the backyard was reduced to allow production to constantly perform construction for competitions but still allow 24/7 access for the HouseGuests.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-59) For the celebrity version of America's Favorite HouseGuest,
texts.12: the term Favorite Celebrity HouseGuest was also being used interchangeably.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-60)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-61) For the first time since the beginning of the American series, five players were featured in the season's finale night versus the usual three.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-62)
texts.13: The main television coverage of _Celebrity Big Brother_ was screened on CBS during the winter of the 2017–18 network television season. CBS decided to schedule the spin-off during the February 2018 sweeps period to counterprogramNBC's coverage of the 2018 Winter Olympics.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Press1-49) Episodes aired on Sundays, Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays with two special episodes on Thursday, February 8 and Saturday, February 24. Most episodes aired for one hour and aired from 8:00–9:00 p.m. EST; the Friday episodes and the season finale, however, ran for two hours each (from 8:00–10:00 p.m. EST).[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Air_dates-63) The live Internet feeds returned for the American version of _Celebrity Big Brother_ as part of CBS All Access.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Press1-49)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-InterviewTHR-46) Alongside the weekly shows on CBS, the companion series _Big Brother: After Dark_ returned on Pop under the title _Celebrity Big Brother: After Dark_. The show provided live coverage nightly from inside the House.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Press1-49)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-64)

_**Celebrity Big Brother**_, also known as _**Big Brother: Celebrity Edition**_,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-1) is a spin-off series of the American version of the Dutch reality television franchise _Big Brother_. This season aired during the winter of the 2017–18 network television season on CBS and was the second American _Big Brother_ season to air outside the usual summer television season, the first being _Big Brother 9_ in 2008. Julie Chen returned as host, with Allison Grodner and Rich Meehan returning as executive producers. The series is produced by Fly on the Wall Entertainment in association with Endemol Shine North America. The first season premiered on February 7, 2018.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-tvline-2)

The promotional logo was released on December 20, 2017. The logo is similar to that used for _Big Brother 19_, with the word "celebrity" added.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-3) The first teaser was also released the same day.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-4) In January 2018 official photos of the house and backyard were released through a press release and an Instagram livestream with Julie Chen.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-6) On January 28, 2018, the official cast was announced during the 60th Annual Grammy Awards.
The first season officially concluded on February 25, 2018, when Marissa Jaret Winokur beat Ross Mathews by a final jury vote of 6 to 3. Ross was also later named _America's Favorite HouseGuest_.
On May 12, 2018, CBS renewed the spin-off for a second season.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-7)

After the first season of the British version of _Big Brother_ proved to be a success in the ratings for Channel 4, the network collaborated with the BBC for the first British season of _Celebrity Big Brother_ in aid of Comic Relief. The season ran for a condensed run of eight days and featured six British celebrities moving into the house used for the first British season.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-42) Due to the success of the first celebrity edition, a second season was ordered and shown exclusively on Channel 4 in November 2002. The celebrity version took a two-year break before returning for its third season in 2005, and became a regular staple alongside the regular British version. Starting with the third season, the show began to feature celebrities outside the United Kingdom alongside well known British celebrities. Many notable American celebrities have since taken part in the British version of _Celebrity Big Brother_.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-GlobalTV-43)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-AmericansInUKCBB-2-44) American actor Gary Busey took part in the fourteenth season in the summer of 2014 and became the first American celebrity to win _Celebrity Big Brother_ in the United Kingdom._[citation needed_]

An American version of _Celebrity Big Brother_ has been speculated since 2002, along with a celebrity version of _Survivor._[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-CBB-2002-1-45) In an interview, Julie Chen and CBS CEO Leslie Moonves revealed talks of a celebrity edition of _Big Brother_ as far back as _Big Brother 2._[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-InterviewTHR-46) It was rumored that CBS was looking to air a celebrity edition in the fall after _Big Brother 3_ with radio personality Howard Stern speculated as a possible houseguest.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-CBB-2002-2-47) Chen revealed that Paris Hilton had agreed to do it and Roseanne Barr initially agreed to take part, but then backed out.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-InterviewTHR-46) Barr would later take part in another celebrity spin-off of _Big Brother_ called _Big Brother: Celebrity Hijack_ in the United Kingdom in 2008, where she watched over a group of non-celebrity housemates for a day, set tasks and talked to them in the Diary Room.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Roseanne-BBCH-48)

Julie Chen announced on September 7, 2017, during a live double eviction episode of _Big Brother 19_ that _Celebrity Big Brother_ would air sometime during the winter, before the twentieth season of _Big Brother_ in the summer of 2018. CBS later confirmed via a press release that Julie Chen would return to host the new season, and Allison Grodner and Rich Meehan will be executive producers. The season will be produced by Fly on the Wall Entertainment in association with Endemol Shine North America.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Press1-49)
On September 13, 2017, it was revealed by Chen that her husband, CBS chief executive Leslie Moonves, forced her to take a pay cut for the celebrity edition to happen. Moonves stated, "You shouldn't be expected to be paid as if it's a full series. It's a condensed version."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-tvguide-50)
The format of the show remained similar to the American version of _Big Brother_. Competitions for Head of Household and Power of Veto had been confirmed to returned for this edition along with live evictions.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-tvline-2) On December 1, 2017, CBS revealed that the series would premiere on February 7, 2018, and wrap on February 25, 2018.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-51)

_Celebrity Big Brother_ was a condensed version of the game and would not last as long as a regular season of _Big Brother_, with episodes only shown over two weeks instead of three months.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-tvguide-50)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-52) Unlike the parent series Jury members were not sequestered separately and were allowed to return to the outside world as well as watch the show.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-53)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-54) Beginning with an incident that led to a lawsuit in _Big Brother 2_ when HouseGuest Justin Sebik got drunk and threatened fellow HouseGuest Krista Stegall by holding a knife to her throat, there has been an alcohol restriction in the house.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-55)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-56) The alcohol restriction was lifted for the Celebrity HouseGuests.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-57)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-58) The space in the backyard was reduced to allow production to constantly perform construction for competitions but still allow 24/7 access for the HouseGuests.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-59) For the celebrity version of America's Favorite HouseGuest,

the term Favorite Celebrity HouseGuest was also being used interchangeably.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-60)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-61) For the first time since the beginning of the American series, five players were featured in the season's finale night versus the usual three.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-62)

The main television coverage of _Celebrity Big Brother_ was screened on CBS during the winter of the 2017–18 network television season. CBS decided to schedule the spin-off during the February 2018 sweeps period to counterprogramNBC's coverage of the 2018 Winter Olympics.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Press1-49) Episodes aired on Sundays, Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays with two special episodes on Thursday, February 8 and Saturday, February 24. Most episodes aired for one hour and aired from 8:00–9:00 p.m. EST; the Friday episodes and the season finale, however, ran for two hours each (from 8:00–10:00 p.m. EST).[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Air_dates-63) The live Internet feeds returned for the American version of _Celebrity Big Brother_ as part of CBS All Access.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Press1-49)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-InterviewTHR-46) Alongside the weekly shows on CBS, the companion series _Big Brother: After Dark_ returned on Pop under the title _Celebrity Big Brother: After Dark_. The show provided live coverage nightly from inside the House.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-Press1-49)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_1_(American_season)#cite_note-64)

"Big Brother" Season 28 will air on CBS and will be available to stream on Paramount+ for Premium subscribers. Paramount+ Essential subscribers will be able to catch the episode the day after it airs.

_**Celebrity Big Brother 2**_[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-2) is the second season of the American reality television series _Celebrity Big Brother_, also known as _Big Brother: Celebrity Edition_. It premiered on CBS on January 21, 2019, and concluded on February 13, 2019. It consisted of thirteen episodes, each approximately 60–120 minutes long, with Allison Grodner and Rich Meehan as executive producers for Fly on the Wall Entertainment, in association with Endemol Shine North America. CBS ordered the season on May 12, 2018, and confirmed it for a mid-season return when the network revealed its 2018–19 fall schedule on May 16, 2018. The network confirmed on November 27, 2018, that Julie Chen Moonves would continue her role as host despite media speculation that she may not return after her husband Les Moonves' departure from CBS Corporation due to sexual misconduct allegations against him.

The season followed a group of celebrities, known as HouseGuests, who lived in the _Big Brother_ House under constant surveillance with no contact from the outside world. Periodically the HouseGuests faced eviction while trying to be the last HouseGuest standing and win the grand prize. Tamar Braxton beat Ricky Williams by a unanimous jury vote during the live final. Braxton is the first African-American winner of the United States version of _Big Brother_, and she and Williams made up the first final two who were both African-American. Tom Green was later named America's Favorite HouseGuest.

The interior of the _Celebrity Big Brother_ house has a New York City theme from around the 1940s.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-House-6-57) Each of the bedrooms on the first floor were given their own individual names reflecting their design. The first bedroom has a "5th Avenue" theme inspired by window shopping highlighting "the highest fashion of the '40s" while the second bedroom has a luxury "Hotel" theme. The third bedroom, known as the "Celebrity Building" Bedroom, that was inspired by a famous art deco building named after a car company.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-House-3-54) The kitchen was inspired by some of the finest restaurants in New York City with a "faux French" oven island and a square dining room table. Behind the dining room table cartoon-style pictures of the season one HouseGuests hanging on the wall.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-House-6-57) The bathroom and downstairs lounge area were inspired by the 20th Century Limited passenger train.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-House-4-55) The Head of Household bedroom resembles the backstage of a Broadway show with the head board made from a real theater marquee.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-House-5-56) The upstairs lounge was designed after the Brooklyn Bridge, while the gym area was inspired by the 42nd Street library in Manhattan.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-House-Twitter-58)

The main television coverage of the second season was screened on CBS during the winter of the 2018–19 network television season. The season premiere was on January 21, 2019, with the season finale airing on February 13, 2019.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-CBB2-Schedule-59) Alongside the weekly shows on CBS, the companion series _Celebrity Big Brother: After Dark_ returned on Pop and to provide live coverage nightly from inside the House.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-60)
The format remains largely unchanged from the previous season. HouseGuests are incarcerated in the Big Brother House with no contact to and from the outside world. Periodically, the HouseGuests take part in several compulsory challenges that determine who would win safety and power in the House.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-format-ep1-61) The winner of the Head of Household (HoH) competition is immune from nominations and is instructed to nominate two fellow HouseGuests for eviction.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-Format-1-62) After a HouseGuest became Head of Household, he or she was ineligible to take part in the next Head of Household competition. The winner of the Power of Veto competition wins the right to save one of the nominated HouseGuests from eviction.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-Format-1-62) If the Veto winner exercised the power, the Head of Household then had to nominate another HouseGuest for eviction.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-Format-1-62)

On eviction night, all HouseGuests except for the Head of Household and the nominees voted to evict one of the nominees.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-Format-1-62) Before the voting began, the nominees had the chance to say a final message to their fellow HouseGuests.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-Format-1-62) This compulsory vote is conducted in the privacy of the Diary Room by the host Julie Chen Moonves. In the event of a tie, the Head of Household would break the tie and reveal their vote in front of the other HouseGuests.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-Format-1-62) Unlike other versions of _Big Brother_, the HouseGuests can discuss the nomination and eviction process open and freely.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-63)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-64) The nominee with the most votes from the other HouseGuests is evicted from the House on eviction night and interviewed by the host.

HouseGuests can voluntarily leave the House at any time (referred to as "walking") and those who break the rules are expelled by Big Brother.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-Walking-example-65)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-Expelled-example-66) The evictees of the season form the Jury that vote for the winner on the season finale; they are known as the jury members.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-Format-Jury-67) Unlike the jury members of _Big Brother_, the celebrity jury members are not sequestered after their eviction and are able to watch the show after their eviction.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-format-ep13-68) The winner of _Celebrity Big Brother_ receives the grand prize of $250,000.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-CastPR-53)

_**Celebrity Big Brother**_, also known as _**Big Brother: Celebrity Edition**_, is a reality televisionspin-off series of the American adaptation of _Big Brother_ created by [John de Mol Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_de_Mol_Jr. "John de Mol Jr.") The series began on February 7, 2018, on CBS in the United States and is simulcast in Canada on Global. The series is filmed at CBS Studio Center in sound stage eighteen located in Studio City, Los Angeles. Julie Chen Moonves reprises her role as host from _Big Brother_ with Allison Grodner and Rich Meehan also returning as executive producers. The series is produced by Fly on the Wall Entertainment in association with Endemol Shine North America.
The premise of the series remained largely unchanged from the main edition of _Big Brother_, in which a group of contestants, known as "HouseGuests," who live in a purpose-built house, known as the Big Brother House, with no contact from the outside world. The contestants compete in competitions for safety and for power over the household before voting each other out in an attempt to be the last HouseGuest remaining and win a grand prize. The difference from the parent series is the inclusion of "Celebrity" HouseGuests (those with notoriety prior to participating in the series), the time frame (a month as opposed to 3 months) and a smaller grand prize ($250,000 as opposed to $750,000)
Each season is also transmitted in real-time which allows for greater viewer participation in the form of _America's Vote_ where the public can give their favorite HouseGuest various prizes ranging from luxury items to advantage to help them survive inside the House. Prior to the live season finale, the viewers are able to vote for their _America's Favorite HouseGuest_ with the winner getting an auxiliary prize of $25,000.

The first overall season of _Celebrity Big Brother_ worldwide premiered in the United Kingdom in 2001 while an American version of the format has been speculated since 2002. The first season of the American adaptation was announced during a live double eviction episode of the nineteenth regular season on September 7, 2017, by Julie Chen Moonves. The first season was scheduled during the February 2018 sweeps period to counterprogramNBC's coverage of the 2018 Winter Olympics. The series premiere was the number one program for CBS attracting 7.27 million viewers and the highest-rated season premiere since _Big Brother 13_. The program was often covered in the media due to the inclusion of Omarosa Manigault and her political revelations in the first season.
In September 2021, CBS renewed _Celebrity Big Brother_ for a third season, which premiered on February 2, 2022.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Air_date-1)
In October 2025, CBS cancelled _Celebrity Big Brother_ after three seasons.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-2)

The series is a game show in which a group of celebrity contestants, referred to as HouseGuests, live in a custom-built set, known as the Big Brother House, constantly under video surveillance.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Format-1-3) While in the House, the HouseGuests are completely isolated from the outside world, meaning no phone, television, Internet, magazines, newspaper, or contact with those not in the House.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Format-2-4) This rule could be broken, however, in the event of a medical injury, a family emergency, or death.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Format-2-4) The format of the series is mainly seen as a social experiment, and requires HouseGuests to interact with others who may have differing ideals, beliefs, and prejudices.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Format-3-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Format-3.2-6) Though locked in the House, the HouseGuests are free to quit the game, though will not be allowed entry back into the game.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Format-4-7) Should a HouseGuest break the rules of the game, they could be expelled from the House,

and unable to return.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Format-2-4)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Format-5-8) The HouseGuests compete for a grand prize of $250,000 and the runner-up is awarded $50,000.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Format-1-3)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Format-6-9) Prior to the live finale the viewers are able to award their favorite HouseGuest of the season the title _America's Favorite HouseGuest_ with a cash prize of $25,000.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Format-6-9)
The symbol used for the Power of Veto

### Differences from _Big Brother_
Deena Katz serves as the casting director for the series she also is known for casting ABC's _Dancing with the Stars_.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Casting-42) Grodner revealed she spoke with the producers of the British adaptation about their experiences with celebrities. Due to the American adaptation featuring more competitions than other formats there is no special treatment for the celebrities in order for the competitions "to be as fair as possible".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-43)Tamar Braxton won the second season and became the first ever African-American HouseGuest to win in the history of the American adaptation of _Big Brother_.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-CBB2_Winner-22) In an effort to promote diversity, CBS announced a new rule for _Big Brother_ that 50% of all contestants must be a person of color or an indigenous person for the 2021–2022 broadcast season.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-19 "Big Brother (American TV series)")

### Production design and music
[edit]
_Celebrity Big Brother_ uses a similar title sequence and logo that was introduced with the sixteenth season of _Big Brother_ that was designed by Charlie Co.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Graphics-1-44) The logo was slightly modified to remove the water effects which were replaced by faint lights while the word "Celebrity" before "Big" with "Brother" underneath. The water effect that was used as a transition and appears around the HouseGuests was removed. This was replaced with a star being used as the transition and items related to the celebrities notoriety appeared around them.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-BB19Opening-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-CBB1Opening-46) The series also uses the same theme song as _Big Brother_ during the opening title sequence which was composed by David Vanacore and Ken Berry.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-ClosingCredits-36)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-BB19Opening-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-CBB1Opening-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-47)
A view of CBS Studio Center sound stage 18, where the house is located

### Production design and music
Filming for the series takes place at CBS Studio Center, sound stage eighteen where the sitcom _Yes, Dear_ was filmed.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-House-1-48)_Celebrity Big Brother_ is filmed in the same location as _Big Brother_ since its sixth season and is referred to as the _Big Brother House_ often shortened to _House_.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-House-2-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-House-3-50) The House has 94 high-definition cameras and over 113 microphones in order to monitor and record the HouseGuests.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-CBS-CBB2-PR-51) The first floor of the House consists of three bedrooms, storage room and the Diary Room which is accessible by the living room. The bathroom, a lounge room, backyard and a spiral staircase going to the second floor are accessed via the kitchen. The front door is located in a vestibule area that separates the living room and kitchen. The Head of Household bedroom and en suite bathroom is located on the second floor. The second floor also has a balcony with an additional lounge area where the HouseGuests can look down and see the first floor. The backyard is significantly smaller due to the majority of the backyard being used for constant competitions.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-House-4-52) During _Celebrity Big Brother_ a roof is installed over the backyard.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-53) The pool table was brought inside from the backyard and moved to the upstairs lounge area.

### Production design and music
The spare room sometimes used for tasks on the civilian _Big Brother_ series, such as the Den of Temptation in season nineteen, is turned into an indoor gym for the celebrity edition.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-CBB1-House-54)
After the success of the first season CBS ordered a second season to air during the winter of the 2018–19 television season on May 12, 2018.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-55) The network reconfirmed the news four days later when the network revealed its 2018–19 fall prime-time schedule.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-56) After the departure of Les Moonves from CBS Corporation on September 9, 2018, because of multiple sexual misconduct allegations, the media speculated that Julie Chen Moonves might not continue hosting _Celebrity Big Brother_ and _Big Brother_.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-57) CBS later confirmed on November 27, 2018 that Chen Moonves would host the second season of the series.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-JCReturn-35)

### Production design and music
_Celebrity Big Brother_ was not mentioned when CBS announced their plans for the 2019–20 television season on May 15, 2019.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-59)Kelly Kahl, president of entertainment at CBS, revealed on May 21, 2019 that a third season of the celebrity spin-off is still uncertain.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-60) On September 5, 2019 the parent series _Big Brother_ was renewed for a twenty-second season with Chen Moonves signing a new contract to return as host.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-61) However the new contract for Chen Moonves did not include a future season of _Celebrity Big Brother_ with CBS not announcing anything official regarding the series.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-62) On November 11, 2019, CBS announced their 2020 winter schedule, which did not include _Celebrity Big Brother_.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-63) On December 28, 2020, Chen Moonves revealed that shortly after the conclusion of the twenty-second season of the civilian version of _Big Brother_ that she and numerous producers pushed CBS to order a third season of _Celebrity Big Brother_ but that they declined to order one at the time leaving the option open to still order a third season at a later date.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-64)

_**Celebrity Big Brother 2**_[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-2) is the second season of the American reality television series _Celebrity Big Brother_, also known as _Big Brother: Celebrity Edition_. It premiered on CBS on January 21, 2019, and concluded on February 13, 2019. It consisted of thirteen episodes, each approximately 60–120 minutes long, with Allison Grodner and Rich Meehan as executive producers for Fly on the Wall Entertainment, in association with Endemol Shine North America. CBS ordered the season on May 12, 2018, and confirmed it for a mid-season return when the network revealed its 2018–19 fall schedule on May 16, 2018. The network confirmed on November 27, 2018, that Julie Chen Moonves would continue her role as host despite media speculation that she may not return after her husband Les Moonves' departure from CBS Corporation due to sexual misconduct allegations against him.

The season premiere was on January 21, 2019, with the season finale airing on February 13, 2019.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-CBB2-Schedule-59) Alongside the weekly shows on CBS, the companion series _Celebrity Big Brother: After Dark_ returned on Pop and to provide live coverage nightly from inside the House.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-60)
The format remains largely unchanged from the previous season. HouseGuests are incarcerated in the Big Brother House with no contact to and from the outside world. Periodically, the HouseGuests take part in several compulsory challenges that determine who would win safety and power in the House.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-format-ep1-61) The winner of the Head of Household (HoH) competition is immune from nominations and is instructed to nominate two fellow HouseGuests for eviction.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-Format-1-62) After a HouseGuest became Head of Household, he or she was ineligible to take part in the next Head of Household competition. The winner of the Power of Veto competition wins the right to save one of the nominated HouseGuests from eviction.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-Format-1-62) If the Veto winner exercised the power, the Head of Household then had to nominate another HouseGuest for eviction.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-Format-1-62)

In the event of a tie, the Head of Household would break the tie and reveal their vote in front of the other HouseGuests.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-Format-1-62) Unlike other versions of _Big Brother_, the HouseGuests can discuss the nomination and eviction process open and freely.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-63)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_2_(American_season)#cite_note-64) The nominee with the most votes from the other HouseGuests is evicted from the House on eviction night and interviewed by the host.

texts.1:
_**Celebrity Big Brother**_, also known as _**Big Brother: Celebrity Edition**_, is a reality televisionspin-off series of the American adaptation of _Big Brother_ created by [John de Mol Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_de_Mol_Jr. "John de Mol Jr.") The series began on February 7, 2018, on CBS in the United States and is simulcast in Canada on Global. The series is filmed at CBS Studio Center in sound stage eighteen located in Studio City, Los Angeles. Julie Chen Moonves reprises her role as host from _Big Brother_ with Allison Grodner and Rich Meehan also returning as executive producers. The series is produced by Fly on the Wall Entertainment in association with Endemol Shine North America.
The premise of the series remained largely unchanged from the main edition of _Big Brother_, in which a group of contestants, known as "HouseGuests," who live in a purpose-built house, known as the Big Brother House, with no contact from the outside world. The contestants compete in competitions for safety and for power over the household before voting each other out in an attempt to be the last HouseGuest remaining and win a grand prize. The difference from the parent series is the inclusion of "Celebrity" HouseGuests (those with notoriety prior to participating in the series), the time frame (a month as opposed to 3 months) and a smaller grand prize ($250,000 as opposed to $750,000)
Each season is also transmitted in real-time which allows for greater viewer participation in the form of _America's Vote_ where the public can give their favorite HouseGuest various prizes ranging from luxury items to advantage to help them survive inside the House. Prior to the live season finale, the viewers are able to vote for their _America's Favorite HouseGuest_ with the winner getting an auxiliary prize of $25,000.
texts.2:
The first overall season of _Celebrity Big Brother_ worldwide premiered in the United Kingdom in 2001 while an American version of the format has been speculated since 2002. The first season of the American adaptation was announced during a live double eviction episode of the nineteenth regular season on September 7, 2017, by Julie Chen Moonves. The first season was scheduled during the February 2018 sweeps period to counterprogramNBC's coverage of the 2018 Winter Olympics. The series premiere was the number one program for CBS attracting 7.27 million viewers and the highest-rated season premiere since _Big Brother 13_. The program was often covered in the media due to the inclusion of Omarosa Manigault and her political revelations in the first season.
In September 2021, CBS renewed _Celebrity Big Brother_ for a third season, which premiered on February 2, 2022.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Air_date-1)
In October 2025, CBS cancelled _Celebrity Big Brother_ after three seasons.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-2)
texts.3: The series is a game show in which a group of celebrity contestants, referred to as HouseGuests, live in a custom-built set, known as the Big Brother House, constantly under video surveillance.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Format-1-3) While in the House, the HouseGuests are completely isolated from the outside world, meaning no phone, television, Internet, magazines, newspaper, or contact with those not in the House.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Format-2-4) This rule could be broken, however, in the event of a medical injury, a family emergency, or death.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Format-2-4) The format of the series is mainly seen as a social experiment, and requires HouseGuests to interact with others who may have differing ideals, beliefs, and prejudices.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Format-3-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Format-3.2-6) Though locked in the House, the HouseGuests are free to quit the game, though will not be allowed entry back into the game.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Format-4-7) Should a HouseGuest break the rules of the game, they could be expelled from the House,

Filming for the series takes place at CBS Studio Center, sound stage eighteen where the sitcom _Yes, Dear_ was filmed.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-House-1-48)_Celebrity Big Brother_ is filmed in the same location as _Big Brother_ since its sixth season and is referred to as the _Big Brother House_ often shortened to _House_.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-House-2-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-House-3-50) The House has 94 high-definition cameras and over 113 microphones in order to monitor and record the HouseGuests.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-CBS-CBB2-PR-51) The first floor of the House consists of three bedrooms, storage room and the Diary Room which is accessible by the living room. The bathroom, a lounge room, backyard and a spiral staircase going to the second floor are accessed via the kitchen. The front door is located in a vestibule area that separates the living room and kitchen. The Head of Household bedroom and en suite bathroom is located on the second floor. The second floor also has a balcony with an additional lounge area where the HouseGuests can look down and see the first floor. The backyard is significantly smaller due to the majority of the backyard being used for constant competitions.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-House-4-52) During _Celebrity Big Brother_ a roof is installed over the backyard.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_Big_Brother_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-53) The pool table was brought inside from the backyard and moved to the upstairs lounge area.
